context: Bitter sarcasm. Dante has just met five Florentine nobles among the thieves, and congratulates his city on being famous even in Hell.

quote: beating your wings over sea and land
note: An echo of Florence's own boasting. A Latin inscription of 1255 on the city's palace of government, now the Bargello, praised Florence as mistress of sea and land.
The thieves of Canto 25: Cianfa, Agnello, Buoso, Puccio and Francesco.
An old belief, found in classical poets, that dreams dreamed just before waking come true. Dante's three dreams on the mountain of Purgatory all come at dawn.

A small town ten miles from Florence and under its thumb: even the nearest neighbor wishes the city harm. Others see Cardinal Niccolò da Prato, who came to make peace in Florence in 1304, failed, and left the city under his curse. A bridge collapse and a great fire followed that year.

quote: it will grieve me more as I grow older
note: A hard line. Probably: the punishment must come, and the longer it is delayed, the harder it will be for an aging exile to watch his city suffer.
The souls in this ditch were brilliant men who misused their minds. Dante knows his own gift is of the same kind, and what he saw here makes him hold it in check.
Dante was born under Gemini, the constellation he credits with his talent in Paradiso 22. The "better force" is the grace of God.

quote: hides his face least from us
note: Summer, when the days are longest. The next line gives the hour: dusk, when the flies go and the mosquitoes come out.

Its sinners are traditionally called the evil counsellors, from the charge of "fraudulent advice" in Canto 27. Dante never names the sin directly. Many readers define it more broadly, as the use of a brilliant mind and a persuasive tongue to deceive.
The Hebrew prophet who succeeded Elijah. When a crowd of boys mocked his bald head, he cursed them, and two bears came out of the woods and mauled forty-two of them (2 Kings 2:23–24).

The prophet Elijah was carried up to heaven in a chariot of fire while Elisha watched (2 Kings 2:11–12). Dante imagines the chariot shrinking to a point of flame in the sky, with nothing of the man visible.

quote: none reveals what it steals away
note: The Italian word is theft. Each flame hides its sinner like stolen goods, as these men hid their true purposes in life.

quote: each wraps himself in what burns him
note: They sinned with the tongue, and each is now a tongue of fire that speaks only by flickering. The Letter of James calls the tongue itself a fire (James 3:6).

Eteocles and Polynices, sons of Oedipus, fought over the throne of Thebes and killed each other. When they were burned on one pyre the flame split in two, as if they hated each other even in death. The story is in the Thebaid of Statius.

context: He shares his flame with his old partner Diomedes. Virgil lists three of the deceits they carried out together.

note: A Greek king and one of the best fighters at Troy. In the ancient stories he is Ulysses's companion in night raids and tricks.

The Greeks pretended to sail home and left a huge wooden horse full of soldiers. The Trojans dragged it into the city, and Troy fell that night. Aeneas escaped the ruin and his descendants founded Rome, so the trick was also the "door" through which Rome's ancestors went out.

Achilles's mother hid him on the island of Scyros, dressed as a girl, to keep him from the war. There he loved the king's daughter Deidamia. Ulysses and Diomedes came disguised as merchants and exposed him by laying weapons among their wares. He left her for Troy, where he died.
A sacred statue of the goddess Pallas Athena, kept in Troy. The city could not fall while it was there. Ulysses and Diomedes crept in and stole it.
Much debated. Virgil may mean that proud Greek heroes would look down on a modern Italian, while he, an ancient poet who wrote of their war, has a claim on them. Dante also knew no Greek.
The Aeneid. It is a bold appeal, since Virgil's poem takes the Trojan side and has nothing good to say of Ulysses.

quote: where he went, lost, to meet his death
note: Homer's Odyssey, in which Ulysses comes home to Ithaca, could not be read in western Europe in Dante's time. The story that follows, of a last voyage into the unknown ocean, is as far as anyone knows Dante's own invention.
Ulysses, the more famous of the two. Diomedes never speaks.

The enchantress who turned Ulysses's men into pigs. He stayed with her for a year. Dante knew the story from Ovid and Virgil. Her home was placed on the Italian coast at Monte Circeo, between Rome and Naples.

context: Aeneas named Gaeta, a port near Circe's mountain, after his old nurse Caieta, who died there (Aeneid 7). Ulysses passed that way first. The two heroes are set side by side: Aeneas is the model of duty to father, son and people, and Ulysses is about to say he put all three aside.

note: Telemachus. The father in the next line is Laertes.
The wife of Ulysses, who waited faithfully for him through the ten years of the war and the ten of his wanderings.

context: The two heights on either side of the Strait of Gibraltar, where the Mediterranean meets the Atlantic. They marked the limit of the world that people were meant to know.

note: A city on the African shore of the strait, facing Gibraltar. With Seville on the Spanish side, it is the last of the known world.
Medieval geography held that all the land was in the northern half of the globe. The southern half was thought to be nothing but ocean.
The short waking time of the senses that is left to them: what remains of their lives.

quote: you weren't made to live like animals
note: Among the most quoted lines in Italian: "fatti non foste a viver come bruti, ma per seguir virtute e canoscenza". The call is noble, and it is also the speech of a deceiver leading tired old men to their deaths. Readers have always been divided between Ulysses the hero of knowledge and Ulysses the false counsellor.

quote: Turning our stern toward the dawn
note: With their backs to the east, they row west, out into the Atlantic.
In Italian, folle volo. Ulysses judges his own voyage. Dante used the same word, folle, in Inferno 2, when he feared his own journey might be madness. His has heaven's leave. Ulysses's did not.

quote: always gaining on the left side
note: Bearing steadily to port, so their course runs southwest.
They have crossed the equator. The stars around the south pole are all in view, and the North Star has sunk below the horizon.
Five full moons: they have been on the open ocean for five months.

context: The mountain of Purgatory, the only land in the southern ocean. Ulysses never learns what he has seen. Dante will reach its shore in Purgatorio 1, and remarks there that no one who sailed those waters ever returned.

note: An echo of the storm in the first book of the Aeneid, where a wave spins a ship around three times before the sea swallows it.
God. Ulysses, a pagan, does not know the name of the power that sank him. No living man may reach that shore by his own strength.
